The rain stopped at five in the morning. When Lin Zhao pushed up the shutter of the watch repair shop, the neon at the mouth of the alley was still lit, and a broken sign trembled in the puddle: TIME CAN BE MENDED.

She didn't believe it. Her father had been missing for three years, leaving behind only half a charred pocket watch and a note that read "Stay away from the clock tower." But today the watch suddenly started to run on its own, and every time the second hand ticked, something tapped softly on the back wall of the shop, like someone knocking from inside.

Lin Zhao pulled apart the old cabinet and found a roll of film hidden behind the bricks. It showed her father when he was young, standing on the top floor of the abandoned clock tower. He told the camera that every stormy night the city lost one person, because the old machine inside the tower could steal a person's day. The stolen time was sold to the richest people in town.

At the end of the reel, her father looked back into the darkness and whispered, "Little Zhao, if you are seeing this, it means it has started turning again."

At noon, the property developer Gu Zhun came to the shop with his men and announced that the whole old street would be demolished tomorrow. Lin Zhao recognized the gold watch on his cuff: in the middle of its dial was the same gear as in her father's watch. Gu Zhun smiled and slid the compensation agreement across the counter. "Sign it. Old things can't be kept."

Lin Zhao did not sign. She pressed the pocket watch against the agreement, and the second hand suddenly ran backwards while every clock in the room stopped at once. Gu Zhun's face changed and he reached to snatch it. She stepped aside and saw a long, thin pendulum in his shadow, slicing the light on the floor again and again.

In that moment she finally understood that her father's warning had never been telling her to run, but to wait until the watch woke up. She closed the shop door, tucked the film into her pocket, and set off for the clock tower in the north of the city. The rain clouds pressed back down over the skyline, and at the first clap of thunder every streetlight went out.
